problems.title: Rectangular rosette beside a fuselage window
problems.setup: A 0°/45°/90° rectangular strain rosette is bonded to the aluminium skin (E = 70 GPa, ν = 0.33, plane stress) beside a cabin window cutout of a light aircraft. Gauge a lies along x, gauge b at 45° counterclockwise from x, gauge c along y. Under a pressurization test the gauges read ε_a = 600 µε, ε_b = 400 µε, ε_c = −200 µε. Use the small strain transformation ε(θ) = ε_xx cos²θ + ε_yy sin²θ + γ_xy sinθ cosθ with engineering shear strain γ_xy.
problems.x: A rosette gives three normal strains, the transformation law turns them into ε_xx, ε_yy and γ_xy, and Mohr's circle of strain (radius √(((ε_xx − ε_yy)/2)² + (γ_xy/2)²)) gives the principal strains and directions.

parts.ask: Find the engineering shear strain γ_xy from the 45° gauge.
Find the major principal strain ε₁.
sol: ε₁ = C + R = 647.2 µε (and ε₂ = C − R = −247.2 µε)

parts.ask: Find the angle θ_p, measured counterclockwise from gauge a, of the ε₁ direction.
sol: check: ε(13.28°) = 647.2 µε, the major value

parts.ask: On Mohr's circle of strain, how is the gauge rotation θ represented, and what is plotted on the vertical axis?
parts.a: A rotation of 2θ around the circle, with γ/2 on the vertical axis
w: A rotation of θ around the circle, with γ on the vertical axis
A rotation of 2θ around the circle, with γ on the vertical axis
A rotation of θ/2 around the circle, with γ/2 on the vertical axis
sol: The tensor shear strain ε_xy = γ_xy/2 transforms with ε_xx and ε_yy
Physical angle θ maps to 2θ on the circle

parts.ask: Examiner twist: the rosette only sees in-plane strains. Using plane stress, find the through-thickness strain ε_zz.
sol: ε_zz = −197.0 µε, so the skin thins slightly

problems.title: Inflatable habitat bladder: Cauchy to Piola stresses
problems.setup: A patch of the rubber gas bladder of an inflatable habitat module is in plane stress. Its deformation gradient and Cauchy stress (MPa) at a point are F = [[2, 0.5, 0],[0, 1, 0],[0, 0, 0.5]] and σ = [[4, 1, 0],[1, 2, 0],[0, 0, 0]]. Use P = JσF⁻ᵀ and S = F⁻¹P = JF⁻¹σF⁻ᵀ, with J = det F.
problems.x: Cauchy stress is force per current area, the first Piola stress P = JσF⁻ᵀ is current force per reference area, and the second Piola stress S = F⁻¹P is the symmetric, rotation invariant measure that pairs with the Green strain.

parts.ask: Find the component P₁₁ of the first Piola stress.
Find S₁₁ of the second Piola stress.
A reference face with normal N = e₁ has reference area dA = 200 mm². Find the magnitude of the force it carries in the deformed state.
sol: df = P N dA (first Piola maps reference area to current force)
check with Nanson: n da = JF⁻ᵀN dA = (100, −50, 0) mm², σ(n da) = (350, 0, 0) N

parts.ask: Here P₁₂ = 1 MPa while P₂₁ = 0. Which statement is correct?
parts.a: P is a two point tensor, so it is generally unsymmetric while σ and S are symmetric
w: The Cauchy stress has an error, because angular momentum balance makes P symmetric
S inherits the asymmetry of P, so S₁₂ ≠ S₂₁
P is symmetric only when J = 1, so this F has J ≠ 1
sol: Angular momentum balance gives σ = σᵀ, equivalently PFᵀ = FPᵀ
P has one leg in the current and one in the reference configuration
S = F⁻¹P is symmetric: here S is diagonal

parts.ask: Examiner twist: after deforming, the patch is rigidly rotated by 90° about e₃, Q = [[0, −1, 0],[1, 0, 0],[0, 0, 1]], so F* = QF and σ* = QσQᵀ. Find σ*₁₁.
sol: σ* = QσQᵀ swaps the in-plane axes: σ*₁₁ = σ₂₂ = 2 MPa
P* = J σ* F*⁻ᵀ = QP (rotates with the body)

problems.title: Bolted combustor rail: thin plate versus thick block
problems.setup: A nickel alloy mounting rail for a combustor liner (E = 200 GPa, ν = 0.3, α = 13 × 10⁻⁶ /K, elevated temperature yield σ_y = 480 MPa) is bolted rigidly at both ends along x₁, so ε₁₁ = 0. The faces normal to x₂ are free (σ₂₂ = 0). It is heated uniformly by ΔT = 150 K. Use ε_ij = ((1 + ν)/E)σ_ij − (ν/E)σ_kk δ_ij + αΔT δ_ij.
problems.x: Each added constraint raises thermal stress: one restrained direction gives −EαΔT, and a thick section that is also held in x₃ (plane strain) gives σ₁₁ = σ₃₃ = −EαΔT/(1 − ν).

parts.ask: Thin rail (plane stress, σ₃₃ = 0): find σ₁₁.
sol: ε₁₁ = σ₁₁/E + αΔT = 0 with σ₂₂ = σ₃₃ = 0

parts.ask: Thin rail: find the free strain ε₂₂ across the width.
sol: ε₂₂ = 2535 µε (Poisson expansion adds to thermal expansion)

parts.ask: Now the rail is a thick block held in x₃ as well (plane strain, ε₃₃ = 0). Which expression gives σ₃₃?
w: σ₃₃ = νσ₁₁
σ₃₃ = ν(σ₁₁ + σ₂₂) + EαΔT
σ₃₃ = 0
sol: the isothermal rule σ₃₃ = ν(σ₁₁ + σ₂₂) gains the thermal term

parts.ask: Thick block: find σ₁₁.
sol: σ₁₁ = −EαΔT/(1 − ν) = −390/0.7 = −557.1 MPa, and σ₃₃ = σ₁₁

parts.ask: Examiner twist: check von Mises yield for both cases with σ_y = 480 MPa.
parts.a: The thin rail stays elastic (390 MPa) and the thick block yields (557 MPa)
w: Both stay elastic, because hydrostatic compression never yields a metal
Both yield, because 390 MPa times √3 exceeds 480 MPa
The thin rail yields and the thick block stays elastic, because σ₃₃ relieves σ₁₁
sol: thin: one nonzero stress, σ_vm = 390 MPa < 480
thick: σ₁₁ = σ₃₃ = −557.1, σ₂₂ = 0, σ_vm = 557.1 MPa > 480
the free x₂ direction keeps the state far from hydrostatic, so the thick block yields

problems.title: Shrink-fit turbopump impeller hub
problems.setup: A steel impeller hub (inner radius a = 25 mm, outer radius b = 50 mm, length L = 40 mm) is shrink-fitted onto a solid steel turbopump shaft with radial interference δ = 0.02 mm. Both parts: E = 200 GPa, ν = 0.3, plane stress. Use σ_rr = A − B/r², σ_θθ = A + B/r², and for the same material p = (Eδ/a)(b² − a²)/(2b²).
problems.x: The interface pressure comes from making the hub's radial growth plus the shaft's radial shrinkage equal the interference, and the hub hoop stress peaks at the bore at p(b² + a²)/(b² − a²).

parts.ask: Find the interface pressure p.
Find the hoop stress in the hub at its bore.
sol: hub: Lamé with p_i = p, p_o = 0

parts.ask: What is the stress state in the solid shaft?
parts.a: Uniform σ_rr = σ_θθ = −p everywhere in the shaft
w: σ_rr = −p at the surface, rising to zero at the centre
σ_θθ = +p and σ_rr = −p, like the hub
σ_θθ = −p(b² + a²)/(b² − a²) at the surface
sol: a solid shaft needs finite stress at r = 0, so B = 0
σ_rr = σ_θθ = A = −p, a uniform equal biaxial compression

parts.ask: With friction coefficient μ = 0.15 at the interface, find the torque the fit can carry before slipping.
Examiner twist: the hub is changed to aluminium (E_h = 70 GPa, ν_h = 0.33) with the same steel shaft and δ. Use δ = pa[(1/E_h)((b² + a²)/(b² − a²) + ν_h) + (1/E_s)(1 − ν_s)]. Find p.
sol: p = (0.02/25)/(3.202 × 10⁻⁵) = 24.98 MPa, the softer hub roughly halves the pressure and the torque

problems.title: Mooney-Rivlin hatch seal tube with held ends
problems.setup: A long silicone tube for an inflatable spacecraft hatch seal is modelled as an incompressible Mooney-Rivlin membrane, W = C₁(I₁ − 3) + C₂(I₂ − 3), with C₁ = 0.2 MPa and C₂ = 0.05 MPa. Unstretched mean radius R = 20 mm, wall thickness T = 2 mm. The end fittings hold the length fixed (λ_z = 1). It inflates to hoop stretch λ = r/R = 1.5, so λ_r = 1/λ and t = T/λ. Principal Cauchy stresses: σ_i = −q + 2C₁λ_i² − 2C₂λ_i⁻² with σ_rr ≈ 0 across the thin wall.
problems.x: With the ends held, a Mooney-Rivlin tube behaves like a neo-Hookean one with μ = 2(C₁ + C₂), and the pressure p = 2(C₁ + C₂)(T/R)(1 − λ⁻⁴) rises steadily toward a plateau.

parts.ask: Find the hoop Cauchy stress σ_θθ at λ = 1.5.
Find the inflation pressure p at λ = 1.5.
sol: membrane: p = σ_θθ t/r with t = T/λ, r = λR

parts.ask: Find the axial Cauchy stress σ_zz that the end fittings must hold at λ = 1.5.
sol: σ_zz = 0.3472 MPa, tensile: the fittings pull to stop the tube shortening

parts.ask: How does p behave as λ keeps growing with the ends held?
parts.a: p rises monotonically toward 2(C₁ + C₂)T/R = 50 kPa
w: p peaks at λ = 7^(1/6) and then falls, like a balloon
p grows without bound like λ²
p peaks at λ = 1.5 and then falls
sol: as λ → ∞, p → 2(C₁ + C₂)T/R = 0.5 × 0.1 MPa = 50 kPa

parts.ask: Examiner twist: the fittings are released and the ends are capped (closed tube, free length, σ_zz = σ_θθ/2). What happens during pressure-controlled inflation?
parts.a: The pressure reaches a limit point, and a local bulge grows at nearly constant pressure
w: The pressure plateau is unchanged, since only the hoop stress drives inflation
The tube shortens until it buckles axially before any bulge forms
The pressure rises faster, since end caps add axial stiffness
sol: free ends let λ_z grow with pressure, thinning the wall faster
solving σ_θθ = 2σ_zz for λ_z, this tube's pressure peaks near λ_θ ≈ 1.99 at about 43 kPa
past the peak a bulge (aneurysm) propagates, as in a party balloon

problems.title: Throttling feed duct: local plus convective acceleration
problems.setup: Liquid oxygen flows along a converging injector feed duct during a throttle change. A 1D model gives the spatial velocity v₁ = U(t)(1 + x₁/L), v₂ = v₃ = 0, with L = 0.5 m and U(t) = U₀ + βt, U₀ = 20 m/s, β = 100 m/s². Evaluate at x₁ = 0.25 m and t = 0.1 s. Use Dv/Dt = ∂v/∂t + (∇v)v.
problems.x: The material derivative Dv/Dt = ∂v/∂t + (∇v)v gives the acceleration of the particle passing a fixed point in space, and the convective part captures speeding up as a particle moves into a faster region.

parts.ask: Find the local acceleration ∂v₁/∂t.
Find the convective acceleration v₁ ∂v₁/∂x₁.
Find the total particle acceleration a₁ = Dv₁/Dt.
The Lagrangian motion is x₁ = −L + (L + X₁)exp(G(t)/L), with G = U₀t + βt²/2. How does it confirm a₁?
parts.a: ∂²x₁/∂t² at fixed X₁ = (L + x₁)[(U/L)² + β/L] = 2850 m/s²
w: ∂²x₁/∂t² at fixed x₁ = β(1 + x₁/L) = 150 m/s²
∂²x₁/∂t² at fixed X₁ = (L + x₁)(U/L)² = 2700 m/s²
∂x₁/∂t at fixed X₁ = 45 m/s, divided by t = 450 m/s²
sol: differentiate twice holding the particle label X₁ fixed

parts.ask: Examiner twist: at the same instant and point the engine is throttling down, β = −100 m/s² (U still 30 m/s). Find a₁.
sol: a₁ = 2550 m/s²: the flow slows at every fixed point while each particle still speeds up

problems.title: Spinning habitat ring: momentum balance in steady rotation
problems.setup: A rotating space station ring of radius R = 224 m spins about its axis to give 1 g (9.81 m/s²) at the rim. The ring structure is a thin aluminium hoop (ρ = 2700 kg/m³) of cross-section A = 0.05 m². Treat the hoop as a thin ring in uniform rotation with hoop force N and only hoop stress σ = N/A.
problems.x: In steady rotation every particle accelerates toward the axis at ω²R, and momentum balance on a half ring gives hoop tension N = qR with q = (mass per length) ω²R, so self-weight stress is ρω²R² = ρ g R.

parts.ask: Find the spin rate for 1 g at the rim.
Find the hoop stress in the bare ring from its own mass.
sol: half ring: 2N = q·2R with q = ρAω²R
σ = N/A = ρω²R² = ρ g R

parts.ask: The ring also carries habitat modules of 2000 kg per metre of circumference hung from it. Find the hoop stress.
sol: mass per length: ρA + m_p = 135 + 2000 = 2135 kg/m

parts.ask: The spatial velocity field v = ω e₃ × x is steady (∂v/∂t = 0). Why is the ring in tension?
parts.a: The convective term (∇v)v = −ω²x gives each particle an inward acceleration that the hoop tension supplies
w: A steady field has zero particle acceleration, so the tension comes from the modules' weight
The local term ∂v/∂t supplies an outward acceleration that the hoop resists
Rotation produces compression, and tension appears only once the modules are added
sol: ρ a = div σ: the net inward force on each element comes from the curved hoop tension

parts.ask: Examiner twist: for a bare aluminium ring at 1 g with allowable stress 200 MPa, find the largest radius.
sol: R_max = 7551 m, set by specific strength σ/ρ

problems.title: Cross-ply CubeSat panel: A matrix and off-axis stiffness
problems.setup: A deployable CubeSat solar panel substrate is a [0/90]s carbon/epoxy laminate. Ply properties: E₁ = 140 GPa, E₂ = 10 GPa, G₁₂ = 5 GPa, ν₁₂ = 0.3, ply thickness 0.125 mm (total h = 0.5 mm). Use Q₁₁ = E₁/(1 − ν₁₂ν₂₁), Q₂₂ = E₂/(1 − ν₁₂ν₂₁), Q₁₂ = ν₁₂Q₂₂, Q₆₆ = G₁₂, ν₂₁ = ν₁₂E₂/E₁, and A_ij = Σ Q̄_ij,k t_k.
problems.x: The A matrix sums ply stiffnesses through the thickness, a symmetric layup gives B = 0, and the effective modulus E_x = (A₁₁A₂₂ − A₁₂²)/(A₂₂h) comes from inverting A.

parts.ask: Find the ply stiffness Q₁₁.
Find A₁₁ for the laminate.
sol: two 0° plies use Q₁₁, two 90° plies use Q₂₂ in the x direction
A₁₁ = 37.74 GPa·mm = 37.74 kN/mm (A₂₂ = A₁₁, A₁₂ = 1.51 kN/mm)

parts.ask: Find the effective in-plane modulus E_x.
sol: E_x = 75.36 GPa, about the average of the 0° and 90° plies

parts.ask: Why is the symmetric [0/90]s preferred over a [0/90] panel for this flat substrate?
parts.a: Symmetry about the midplane gives B = 0, so cure cooling and in-plane loads leave the panel flat
w: Symmetry makes A₁₆ = A₂₆ = 0, which keeps the panel flat after cure
Symmetry doubles D₁₁, which keeps the panel flat after cure
Symmetry makes the laminate quasi-isotropic, so E_x = E_y = E_45
sol: B_ij = ½ Σ Q̄_ij,k (z_k² − z_(k−1)²) cancels for mirror-image plies
an unsymmetric [0/90] warps into a saddle when cooled from cure

parts.ask: Examiner twist: the panel is loaded along a 45° direction. Find the effective modulus E at 45° (equal to E_x of a [±45]s laminate).
sol: rotate the plies by 45°: Q̄ for ±45° plies, then A and E = 1/(h a₁₁) with a = A⁻¹
load now runs through the matrix in shear
E₄₅ = 17.74 GPa, under a quarter of E_x, so cross-ply panels need ±45° plies for shear and off-axis loads
